title: A hybrid AI framework for hypersonic flow physics: Bridging experiments and numerical simulations
abstract: The characterization of hypersonic flow physics in high-enthalpy regimes is one of the crucial challenges in fluid dynamics, where strong thermochemical non-equilibrium effects, steep gradients, and extreme flow conditions significantly limit both experimental and numerical approaches. Experimental campaigns in facilities such as SPES (Small Planetary Entry Simulator) provide valuable insights into these complex physical phenomena, but are inherently limited by sparse spatial resolution and measurement noise. On the other hand, high-fidelity Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations can resolve detailed flow physics, yet their high computational cost severely restricts their use across wide parametric spaces. To address these limitations, this work introduces a hybrid Artificial Intelligence (AI) framework based on Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) for reconstructing key hypersonic flow field quantities from limited and heterogeneous datasets. The approach combines high-fidelity CFD data with experimental measurements obtained at the SPES facility of the University of Naples Federico II, enabling a physically consistent integration between numerical and experimental representations of the flow. Validation on unseen cases demonstrates that the proposed model accurately predicts the main thermochemical quantities, achieving errors within a ± 10% range. These results highlight the potential of physics-driven, data-integrated AI models as efficient tools for analyzing complex hypersonic flow physics, as well as for supporting the design and optimization of future experimental campaigns.

title: Physics-informed data-driven aerodynamic modeling of distributed propulsion wing with extremely tiny datasets
abstract: Based on the research background of high-performance distributed electric propulsion (DEP) fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), a data-driven aerodynamic modeling method is developed to address the design challenges of propulsion/aerodynamic coupling in the distributed propulsion wing (DPW) configuration which fully integrates the distributed propulsors and wing surfaces. To overcome the issues of limited data and insufficient understanding of physical mechanisms in practical engineering, physical prior knowledge is introduced, and a physics-informed grey-box aerodynamic model, named Focus-VI, is established based on extremely tiny datasets utilizing variational inference and attention mechanisms. Compared with the fully black-box multi-layer perceptron (MLP), Focus-VI demonstrates advantages in higher accuracy, stronger generalization ability, and certain interpretability, and can be effectively applied to the modeling, analysis, and optimization design of DPW.

title: Physics-informed CNN–transformer pointer network for decision-stage task allocation of large-scale airborne electro-optical swarms
abstract: Large-scale task allocation is a key decision-stage problem for airborne electro-optical (EO) swarms performing cooperative sensing, regional search, and target-level monitoring. This problem is challenging because UAV–task assignment must simultaneously handle high-dimensional combinatorial search, EO sensing-geometry constraints, cooperative localization requirements, and low-latency assignment generation. This study develops a physics-informed cooperative allocation framework that incorporates EO range and field-of-view constraints, cooperative localization geometry, regional-search coverage, and target-level threat-aware monitoring. A wedge-product-based geometric metric is introduced to characterize dual-platform passive-localization uncertainty and provide a sensing-geometry-aware basis for UAV–task assignment. To solve the resulting variable-scale assignment problem, a CNN–Transformer Pointer Network (CT-PN) is proposed, where a CNN branch extracts local sequence-level features and a Transformer branch models global assignment dependencies across the mixed UAV–target sequence. Simulation results show that CT-PN achieves a favorable tradeoff between decision quality and computational efficiency. In a representative large-scale scenario with 35 UAVs, CT-PN reduces the average decision cost by 30.6% and 25.2% compared with DQN and LSTM-PN, respectively, while maintaining a 12.4% average cost gap relative to the best-performing Iterated Greedy heuristic with more than a 400-fold computational speedup. A post-assignment noisy-bearing localization evaluation further shows that CT-PN improves cooperative localization feasibility beyond the optimized decision cost. At an angular-noise standard deviation of 0.1° and an error tolerance of one spatial unit, CT-PN achieves valid-and-accurate localization rates of 80.75%, 88.20%, and 85.30% in the small-, medium-, and large-scale scenarios, compared with 25.29%, 54.86%, and 54.09% for LSTM-PN. These results indicate that CT-PN provides a low-latency learning-based task-allocation policy with improved post-assignment sensing feasibility relative to learning-based baselines, while retaining a performance gap relative to computationally expensive heuristic search.

title: Multi-fidelity load reconstruction in drone composite wings using in-service strain measurements
abstract: Accurate reconstruction of aerodynamic loads from sparse strain measurements is a longstanding challenge in structural health monitoring (SHM), particularly for lightweight composite wings in unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) where space and weight constraints limit instrumentation. This work presents a data-efficient pipeline for UAV wing load reconstruction under sparse sensing, explicitly designed to operate with limited experimental data. The proposed framework uses a two-stage approach consisting of multi-objective optimization for sensor placement and a hybrid load reconstruction strategy that combines physics-based (low fidelity) with data-driven (high-fidelity) observations. In the first stage, the optimal strain gauge locations are identified numerically through a Pareto-based optimization that balances the number of sensors against reconstruction accuracy. Then, in the second stage, a multi-fidelity approach is developed for the reconstruction of the aerodynamic loads where a calibration matrix (CM), derived from finite element simulations, is combined with an artificial neural network (ANN) trained on limited experimental data to account for modelling discrepancies and improve prediction fidelity. The framework is validated both numerically and experimentally, using wind tunnel experiments on a composite UAV wing. The results show that the multi-fidelity framework improves load reconstruction relative to the CM-only baseline and is particularly effective when experimental data are limited. With only three wind-tunnel runs used for training, the multi-fidelity model reduced the mean MAE from 8.72 to 4.58 for lift and from 8.94 to 4.08 for drag. For lift, the corresponding mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) decreased from 49.23% to 18.44%. When ten training runs were used, the mean MAE was further reduced from 8.73 to 3.85 for lift and from 8.44 to 3.91 for drag, while the lift MAPE decreased from 47.51% to 12.92%. The proposed framework is also compared against a fully data-driven ANN trained on the same experimental datasets. Across the full data-availability study, the multi-fidelity approach reached accurate and stable predictions with fewer training runs than the ANN, which exhibited higher variability under data-scarce conditions. These results highlight the potential of the proposed framework as a promising basis for SHM and digital twin (DT) applications in aerospace structures.

title: A physics-informed constrained gated low-rank adaptation framework for remaining useful life prediction of aeroengines
abstract: Remaining useful life (RUL) prediction for aeroengines is a key to accurately monitoring health status. However, existing methods have generally failed to model RUL prediction from an integrated perspective that accounts for empirical degradation, state decoupling, and operating-condition analysis. Furthermore, a persistent challenge lies in balancing data-driven cross-domain adaptability with the physics consistency of mechanistic laws. A physics-informed constrained gated low-rank adaptation framework is proposed for cross-domain RUL prediction, in which domain knowledge is decomposed into three complementary components, namely black-box state knowledge, operating-condition contextual knowledge, and physical degradation knowledge. Specifically, an in-structure modulation mechanism is designed to inject black-box state knowledge into sequence representations, while operating-condition contextual knowledge and physical degradation knowledge are explicitly embedded into the backbone network via gating to achieve dynamic feature modulation. To enable parameter-efficient adaptation during knowledge disentanglement, a degradation-progress-gated low-rank adaptation mechanism is proposed, aiming to adapt to the target domain with a minimal number of trainable parameters. Also, a degradation-consistency constraint strategy based on gradient conflict awareness is designed to achieve bidirectional correction of both physical penalties and data loss. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves the best average performance across 12 tasks and exhibits more stable physics consistency on representative tasks.

title: Integration of Shapley additive explanations and genetic algorithms for physics-informed aerodynamic shape optimization
abstract: Aerodynamic shape optimization for aircraft design is constrained by the high cost of high-fidelity CFD evaluations and by the stochastic blindness of conventional genetic mutation operators. This study develops SHAP-GA, a physics-guided evolutionary framework that converts model interpretability into gene-level mutation guidance for airfoil design. A database of 750 airfoils is constructed by using the UIUC airfoil archive only as the initial geometry source; each profile is reconstructed with 12 CST coefficients and re-evaluated using a validated ANSYS Fluent workflow at Mach numbers (Ma) of 0.2, 0.4, and 0.6 and an angle of attack (α) of 4°. The resulting CFD-labeled data are used to train a DNN surrogate with a test MRE of 0.647%. SHAP values extracted from the surrogate are transformed into online mutation guidance through a fifth-order Feature-SHAP Fitting mechanism with O(1) query cost and a sparse Norm-ReLU activation that suppresses detrimental geometric states while amplifying beneficial ones. In the 12-dimensional airfoil problem, the positive SHAP-guided GA consistently reduces fitness evaluations and reaches a peak overall mean improvement rate (OMIR) of 16.07% in the high-subsonic Ma = 0.6 condition. Controlled benchmark diagnostics further show substantial convergence gains, including peak OMIR values of 69.70% on the Rosenbrock valley and 43.90% and 18.42% in 3D and 5D tests, respectively. The interpretation also reveals a physically consistent sensitivity migration: lower-surface coefficients control circulation and aft pressure recovery at Ma = 0.2 and 0.4, whereas upper-surface leading-edge coefficients dominate shock-wave mitigation at Ma = 0.6. These results establish a CFD-validated, interpretable optimization strategy for aerodynamic design.

title: Design, machine learning based optimization, experimental validation and numerical analysis for free vibration of multi-auxetic sandwich structures with porosity-dependent GPL-reinforced core
abstract: This research pioneers multi-auxetic design in sandwich beam/plate structures through convergent integration of graphene platelet-reinforced (GPLR) functionally graded auxetic foams and machine-learning-optimized carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) laminates. Triaxial thermocompression-fabricated GPLR-aluminum cores with experimental temperature-dependent properties interface with inverse-designed laminates to form hierarchical structures exhibiting triaxial negative Poisson's ratio control. Experimental-computational validation confirms unprecedented vibration suppression capabilities, including a maximum of 30.18% natural frequency enhancement over non-auxetic systems, significant nonlinear oscillation attenuation, and superior enhancement effect on functionally graded (FG)-O configuration. Critical parametric analyses reveal non-monotonic frequency dependence on core-to-facesheet ratios and thermal degradation. These multi-auxetic architectures demonstrate transformative potential for aerospace vibration-isolation systems requiring multi-dynamic load adaptability.

title: RaPhy-PINO: An FRF-embedded neural operator for resonance-dominant forced-response prediction in aero-engine rotating blade systems
abstract: Resonance-dominant forced response in aero-engine rotating blade systems is governed by narrow-band frequency response function (FRF) amplification, making repeated vibration-stress screening across excitation, damping, and operating variations computationally expensive. This work proposes RaPhy-PINO, an FRF-embedded neural operator for rapid prediction of peak alternating stress and normalized stress-pattern fields over fatigue-relevant high-risk nodes. A Rational Resonance Layer injects modal-rational FRF topology through speed-interpolated prestressed natural frequencies and damping-aware features, while a Fourier-feature trunk reconstructs localized hotspot gradients. Training labels are generated by a physics-consistent offline–online workflow that retains a reference prestressed spatial modal basis and updates the natural frequencies in the analytical FRF denominators by piecewise-linear interpolation over rotational speed. The method is verified on a controlled cantilever-plate benchmark and demonstrated on a representative fan-blade sector under prescribed non-axisymmetric multi-harmonic excitation. On the plate benchmark, RaPhy-PINO improves damping-shift generalization over physics-agnostic and capacity-matched baselines. On the fan-blade case, it predicts peak stress with 𝑅2=0⁢.9997, RMSE = 2.37 MPa, and MAPE = 0.35%, and reconstructs the selected high-risk field with mean 𝑅2=0.9974, RMSE = 0.60 MPa, and mean relative 𝐿2 error = 0.41%. Independent MSC Nastran SOL 108 direct harmonic-response verification over ten representative cases yields mean peak-stress deviations of 0.63% for MSUM and 1.52% for RaPhy-PINO relative to the full-order FE solutions. A 100,000-sample Monte Carlo study demonstrates its utility for rapid resonance-window uncertainty propagation and uncertainty-aware ranking.

title: Hierarchical model predictive control-guided reinforcement learning for energy management of hybrid-electric distributed propulsion aircraft
abstract: This paper proposes a deployable hierarchical control architecture for mission-level energy management in a series hybrid-electric distributed propulsion (DEP) aircraft, explicitly balancing safety and long-horizon optimality. The architecture integrates model predictive control (MPC) with a reinforcement learning-based Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) agent in a phase-adaptive hierarchical structure. MPC ensures conservative, constraint-aware authority during safety-critical phases (takeoff and climb), while the SAC agent provides fuel- and energy-optimal power allocation in less constrained regimes, particularly cruise. Outputs are continuously blended using flight-phase-dependent weights rather than hard switching, with automatic fallback to MPC-only operation upon SAC degradation. The SAC policy, trained off-policy over full missions, generalizes across conditions while strictly enforcing battery state-of-charge and thermal constraints. The energy management is decoupled from trajectory regulation, avoiding online constrained or optimal inner-loop propulsion or speed control. Aircraft velocity evolves naturally from thrust–drag dynamics, guided by a simple fixed-structure feedback controller enforcing predefined phase-dependent speed targets, preserving physical consistency without online constrained optimization. Results demonstrate that the hierarchical MPC-guided SAC framework achieves superior performance across stability, tracking, and efficiency, yielding an overall score of 0.88. By maintaining small SAC corrections between 0.3 and 0.4 in magnitude, the system ensures robust transitions between control authorities. For a 0.38-hour reference mission, the controller leverages low-demand phases for in-flight battery recharging, delivering 9.79 kWh at a peak power of 103 kW to maximize SOC recovery. Compared to MPC-only benchmarks, the strategy achieves a 5.75% reduction in fuel consumption and a 5.7% decrease in C O 2 emissions for both Jet-A and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF). These findings establish that the integrated framework provides a robust, real-time solution for reducing emissions and extending battery longevity without compromising flight performance.

title: Phase-parameterised gaussian process for predicting UAV aerodynamic loads in operational turbine wakes
abstract: ABSTRACT Operational inspection of wind turbines using uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) is an attractive method for reducing offshore operation and maintenance costs, but robust flight in the turbine near-wake remains challenging due to the presence of strong unsteady disturbances that can degrade stability and quality of the inspection. This paper presents a control-oriented modelling framework for predicting UAV aerodynamic loads in operational turbine wakes with faster-than-real-time capability. A free-vortex-wake representation is used to capture the dominant near-wake physics, and a phase-parameterised Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) surrogate model is employed in a wake-aligned coordinate system to exploit the periodic structure of the induced velocity field. The surrogate model is coupled to a nonlinear, physics-informed rotorcraft flight dynamics model to predict wake-induced force perturbations on a quadrotor UAV. The approach is validated against data obtained from an experimental campaign with a scaled three-bladed turbine and a 250 mm-class quadrotor mounted on a load cell. The relevant data and experimental settings are reported as a reference for future research. Across lateral and vertical traverses in the near wake, the predicted streamwise and vertical force components agree with measurements in both magnitude and trend. A frequency-domain error attribution analysis shows the turbine–UAV interaction component, and the results indicate the measured spectral peaks at the turbine rotational and blade-passing harmonics are consistent with the simulations. The present formulation is primarily intended for wake conditions with coherent low-order periodic content, and its prediction fidelity may degrade under strongly turbulent or weakly phase-coherent inflow. Within this scope, the results demonstrate that phase-parameterised GPR surrogates can provide accurate, data-efficient, uncertainty-aware wake disturbance predictions suitable for real-time simulation platforms supporting UAV autonomy and control development for operational turbine inspection.

title: Physics-informed graph neural networks for forecasting eVTOL-induced traffic state perturbations in real-world road networks
abstract: The anticipated large-scale operation of electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft is expected to induce transient passenger flow shocks in the vicinity of vertiports, the propagation of which must be accurately predicted to enable proactive traffic management. To address the tendency of purely data-driven models to generate physically inconsistent predictions for such sparse shock events, a physics-informed graph temporal network (PI-GTN) is proposed. The framework is built around three complementary components: (1) the Lighthill-Whitham-Richards (LWR) conservation law is generalized to sensor graphs of arbitrary topology via the graph Laplacian operator, and a graph-based conservation residual is constructed; (2) a lightweight architecture with two graph convolutional layers, temporal average pooling, and only approximately 5000 parameters is adopted; and (3) a “physics residual” metric that does not rely on ground-truth labels is introduced to quantify the physical consistency of predictions. The conservation residual is jointly optimized with a data-fitting loss and a spatial smoothness regularizer, forcing the predictions to obey traffic wave propagation physics. Under the simulated conditions, experimental results indicate that PI-GTN reduces the physics residual by 91.2% and the global MAE by 29.5% relative to an LSTM baseline, while in single-feature scenarios the smoothness residual is lowered by approximately two orders of magnitude. The established benchmark and metric provide a reproducible platform and a new evaluation dimension for ground–air coupled traffic prediction.

title: Integrated CFD and machine learning investigation of pressure and temperature distributions on a cone at supersonic and hypersonic Mach numbers
abstract: A comprehensive Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) and Unified Machine Learning (ML) framework is developed to study high-speed flow regimes over a cone. The study evaluates the distributions of total pressure and total temperature along the slant length of the cone for freestream Mach numbers between 4.2 and 6 and semi-cone angles between 2° and 20°. Flow properties are extracted at non-dimensional positions (x/L) across the range 0 to 1 in 0.1 increments. The CFD results show that the cone tip experiences a significant total pressure loss due to intense shock interactions, leading to downstream pressure stabilization. The total temperature shows a gradual change pattern, resulting from both viscous dissipation and boundary-layer growth, which becomes more pronounced with increasing Mach number and larger cone angles. The CFD results are validated against the Taylor-Maccoll theory. The machine learning models use Support Vector Machines (SVMs), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and Ordinal Logistic Regression (OLR) to train on CFD data using k-fold cross-validation method. Later, the models' generalizability was tested on the test dataset. The analysis shows that SVM achieves the best total pressure prediction accuracy, while OLR outperforms other methods in total temperature prediction accuracy. KNN demonstrates moderate accuracy, but it struggles to apply its knowledge to new situations. The combined CFD–ML solution enables researchers to achieve their results with less computational work while delivering accurate predictions. It would serve as a powerful resource for high-speed aerodynamic research and design optimization.

title: A few-shot and physically restorable symbolic regression turbulence model based on normalized general effective-viscosity hypothesis
abstract: Turbulence is a complex, irregular flow phenomenon ubiquitous in natural processes and engineering applications. The Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) method, owing to its low computational cost, has become the primary approach for rapid simulation of engineering turbulence problems. However, the inaccuracy of classical turbulence models constitutes the main drawback of the RANS framework. With the rapid development of data-driven approaches, many data-driven turbulence models have been proposed, yet they still suffer from issues of generalizability and accuracy. In this work, we propose a few-shot, physically restorable, symbolic regression turbulence model based on the normalized general effective-viscosity hypothesis. Few-shot indicates that our model is trained on limited flow configurations spanning only a narrow subset of turbulent flow physics, yet can still outperform the baseline model in substantially different turbulent flows. Physically restorable means our model can nearly revert to the baseline model in regimes satisfying specific physical conditions, using only the symbolic regression training results. The normalized general effective-viscosity hypothesis was proposed in our previous study. Specifically, we first formalize the concept of few-shot data-driven turbulence models. Second, we train our symbolic regression turbulence models using only direct numerical simulation (DNS) data for three-dimensional periodic hill flow slices. Third, we evaluate our models on periodic hill flows, zero pressure gradient flat plate flow, NACA0012 airfoil flows, and NASA Rotor 37 transonic axial compressor flows. One of our symbolic regression turbulence models consistently outperforms the baseline model, and we further demonstrate that this model can nearly revert to baseline behavior in certain flow regimes.

title: Sparse-measurement-constrained full-field stress updating of simulation-trained neural operators for aerospace structures
abstract: Accurate full-field stress prediction for real aerospace load-bearing structures is challenging because finite element (FE) simulations provide dense but biased stress fields, whereas experimental measurements are reliable but sparse. This study proposes a sparse-measurement-constrained full-field stress updating framework for simulation-trained neural operators. A fixed-mesh Fourier neural operator is first trained on FE-generated von Mises stress fields to provide a simulation-informed full-field prior. Sparse sensor measurements are then used to diagnose structured simulation-to-reality discrepancies and guide lightweight updating without retraining the surrogate. For a single-rod component with load-level-dependent discrepancy, a gated affine update selectively corrects low-load errors while preserving reliable medium- and high-load predictions. For a double-rod connected component with spatially heterogeneous discrepancy, a regional inverse distance weighting update propagates sensor residuals to the full field according to structural topology. Validation on two aerospace engine-frame components shows that the proposed updates improve sensor-level consistency and preserve physically meaningful stress-field patterns. In leave-one-sensor-out validation, the Case-1 MAPE is reduced from 6.109% to 4.113%, and the Case-2 MAPE is reduced from 24.328% to 18.022%. The framework provides a practical route for measurement-constrained digital-twin stress evaluation under sparse sensing conditions.

title: ANO-MPFM: An Attention Neural Operator Framework for Multi-physics Collaborative Online Estimation of Integrated Ducted Fan-Motor Systems
abstract: The safe operation of integrated ducted fan-motor systems (DF-MSs) under complex operating conditions critically depends on precise characterization of their aerodynamic and thermal states. In practical scenarios highly constrained sensor placement, combined with the intricate coupling between aerodynamic and thermal states, renders this task particularly challenging. This study proposes an attention neural operator-based multi-physics framework (ANO-MPFM), which seamlessly integrates extensive simulation datasets with in-situ sensor measurements to reconstruct spatially non-uniform multi-physics fields and estimate key performance parameters of DF-MSs, offering enhanced interpretability. A collaborative reconstruction strategy is developed, whereby base field priors guide the accurate inference of complex fields. During this prior knowledge integration, a Galerkin attention block explicitly encodes long-range physical priors across domains. Applied to a representative DF-MS case, using only rotational speed and eight motor temperature measurements as observations, the proposed framework achieves outstanding reconstruction performance, with an overall mean absolute error below 8.93×10-3, an overall coefficient of determination exceeding 0.99, and minimal error fluctuations. The approach outperforms conventional models, particularly in reconstructing complex aerodynamic fields of the ducted fan. Further analysis examining the impact of observation noise and sensor placement indicates that temperature measurement points on the motor housing constitute the most critical sensitive regions influencing reconstruction accuracy. The present study offers valuable technical guidance for state monitoring and the design of robust control strategies for DF-MSs operating under complex environmental conditions.

title: Deep reinforcement learning-based double-layer coordinated output voltage prediction method for lithium battery in unmanned aerial vehicle applications
abstract: Under the dynamic flight conditions of hybrid electric unmanned aerial vehicles(UAVs), frequent fluctuations in demand power can cause pronounced variations in lithium battery output voltage, thereby posing challenges to energy management and flight safety. This study proposes a deep reinforcement learning-based double-layer coordinated output voltage prediction method(DRLDCPM) to improve prediction accuracy and response capability under the dynamic UAV flight conditions. The proposed method employs a double-layer coordinated prediction framework consisting of an upper temporal learning layer and a lower residual correction layer. In the upper layer, a long short-term memory network is employed as a base predictor to capture the time-varying characteristics of lithium battery and generate an initial voltage prediction. In the lower layer, a deep deterministic policy gradient algorithm is designed as a residual corrector to dynamically compensate for the prediction errors. The effectiveness and applicability of the proposed DRLDCPM are demonstrated through comparative experiments with recursive least squares(RLS), sequential quadratic programming(SQP), and long short-term memory-backpropagation neural network(LSTM-BP). Compared with RLS, SQP, and LSTM-BP, the proposed DRLDCPM reduces the mean absolute error by 28.1%, 18.9% and 13.6%, respectively, and the corresponding root mean square error by 32.4%, 30.2% and 18.0%, respectively. The proposed method provides more timely and reliable voltage prediction information, thereby supporting battery state monitoring, energy management, low-voltage warning, and flight safety assurance in hybrid-electric UAVs.

title: Distribution-agnostic robust trajectory optimization via chance-constrained reinforcement learning
abstract: This paper presents a distribution-agnostic robust trajectory-optimization framework based on chance-constrained reinforcement learning. The uncertainty is represented here through initial conditions and process noise, with the only requirement being that it can be sampled. A deterministic nominal trajectory is first computed offline, and reinforcement learning is then used only to robustify that baseline through a structured affine closed-loop correction law comprising a feedforward control adjustment and time-varying feedback gains. Probabilistic feasibility is enforced empirically through rollout-based upper-tail quantiles, while terminal dispersion is regulated through covariance-feasibility penalties. The framework is assessed on two materially different trajectory design problems. The flagship case study is a three-dimensional multi-impulse Earth–Mars transfer, where the learned policy is benchmarked against a recent robust trajectory-optimization reference under Gaussian uncertainty and then evaluated under bounded uniform uncertainty and under process disturbances not seen during training. The second case study is a stochastic atmospheric pinpoint rocket landing problem, used to assess portability to a short-horizon continuous-thrust setting with drag, mass depletion, and glide-slope constraints. The results show that the proposed framework can remain competitive in upper-tail fuel cost while preserving probabilistic feasibility, and that the same robustification scaffold can be carried across heterogeneous spacecraft trajectory planning problems without redesign of its core stochastic-control structure.

title: Multiphysics aeroelastic stability of axially moving functionally graded perovskite‑piezoelectric plates under yawed supersonic flow: A hybrid numerical‑machine learning framework
abstract: In this study, the dynamic behavior of an axially moving functionally graded (FG) plate composed of perovskite and piezoelectric ceramic constituents is examined. The structure is subjected to coupled light illumination, electric field, and yawed supersonic flow. A unified multiphysics-data-driven framework is developed to examine the effects of key parameters, including aspect ratio, boundary conditions, in-plane forces, and variable-stiffness elastic foundations. Stability analysis is carried out to determine divergence and flutter boundaries using the generalized differential quadrature method (GDQM) combined with an eigenvalue solution. In addition, two machine learning models, namely ε-support vector regression (ε-SVR) and artificial neural networks (ANN), are employed as efficient surrogate predictors. Their performance is assessed using parity plots, Bland-Altman analysis, error histograms, and Taylor diagrams. The results reveal that light-induced photostriction and thermal effects significantly reduce aeroelastic stability margins, while increasing the electric field lowers the critical axial speed due to electrostrictive and piezoelectric coupling. Decreasing the material gradient index is shown to mitigate these destabilizing effects. Among the models, the medium-sized ANN and cubic-SVR achieve the highest prediction accuracy, whereas linear-SVR exhibits underfitting behavior. The proposed framework provides an accurate and computationally efficient tool for analyzing vibration and aeroelastic instability of idealized smart FG plates under coupled multiphysics loading conditions and may offer useful insights for the preliminary assessment of advanced aerospace structures.

title: A physics-informed generative framework for predicting symmetry-plane unstart flow evolution in a turbine-based combined-cycle inlet
abstract: Unstart in turbine-based combined-cycle (TBCC) inlets is characterized by highly unsteady shock dynamics and complex flow separation, posing substantial challenges to existing intelligent models for accurate flow prediction. To address this issue, this work proposes a physics-informed multimodal temporal-spatial Diffusion Transformer (PI-MTSDiT) framework for predicting unstart-flow evolution in a TBCC inlet. The model is built upon a Diffusion Transformer backbone, augmented with multimodal conditional injection and an interleaved temporal-spatial attention mechanism to capture long-range dependencies among flow variables. Discrete residuals of the unsteady compressible Navier-Stokes (NS) equations are evaluated using finite-volume operators and incorporated into the training process as physical constraints. With limited training data, the proposed model can predict unstart evolution beyond the training set and capture key flow features unseen in the training data, including flow separation and shock spillage at the cowl lip. Compared with the purely data-driven MTSDiT, Transformer, and convolutional long short-term memory (ConvLSTM) baselines, PI-MTSDiT reduces the average root-mean-square error (RMSE) of the physical fields during unstart evolution by 20.98%, 70.18%, and 81.00%, respectively. For near-wall parameter prediction under the unstart state, the average relative error is reduced by 20%~75%. These results demonstrate that integrating Diffusion Transformer modeling with physics-constrained training provides a promising and efficient framework for enhancing both the extrapolation capability and physical consistency of unstart-flow prediction.

title: Analysis of formation flight aerodynamics using vortex lattice method and convolutional neural networks
abstract: Significant fuel savings can be obtained in formation flight by taking advantage of wake vortices if the relative position of aircraft can be effectively optimized. In this paper, formation flight of a leader and a follower unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) is investigated. The location of the follower UAV is varied relative to the leader while flying at various angles of attack, with the wing sweep angle varied between positive and negative values corresponding to forward-swept and swept-back configurations. An in-house code is developed based on the Vortex Lattice Method (VLM) that incorporates such variations in formation flight and is used in conjunction with machine learning to calculate the resulting aerodynamic coefficients of forces and moments. For doing so, the relative spacing and angles are encoded into a structured input representation and the calculated coefficients by the VLM are used to train a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model. Results show that the maximum drag reduction increases as the angle of attack and sweep angle are increased. For negative sweep angles, however, drag tends to increase due to downwash at certain locations behind the leader UAV, resulting in no drag reduction possibility at those locations. Among all sweep angles studied, the forward-swept configuration is observed to cause pronounced differences in lift and rolling moment coefficients. Similarly, the swept-back configuration with the highest sweep angle gives the largest difference in pitching moment. Comparison of the results from the trained CNN model with those from the VLM code shows that the CNN is capable of providing a quick and satisfactory assessment of the aerodynamic performance of formation flights compared to the VLM and that it can successfully predict the location of the sweet spot for different flight configurations.

title: An adaptive physics-informed graph neural network-based method for aero-engine gas path estimation
abstract: Precise estimation of gas path parameters is essential for effective aero-engine health management, despite the inherent complexity of aero-engine internal structures. A reliable estimation model can be characterized as a virtual sensor. The discrepancy between measured data and the estimates from a reliable model reflects the health status of an aero-engine. This study develops an Adaptive Physics-Informed Graph Neural Network Model, termed API-GNN. The model comprises a directed graph neural network, a temporal feature extraction module, independent processing channels, and a composite loss function. The directed graph neural network improves the physical consistency of the API-GNN through the explicit introduction of physics-based directional constraints. The temporal feature extraction module characterizes multi-scale response delay properties through a parallel heterogeneous network and an explicit memory unit. Independent processing channels enhance the estimation accuracy of the API-GNN by separately addressing distinct flight conditions. The composite loss function improves estimation accuracy while incorporating engineering-informed physical constraints. Furthermore, a local parameter updating strategy enhances the adaptability of the API-GNN, achieving a balance between update efficiency and generalization capability. The API-GNN exhibits superior predictive performance to conventional methods over the aero-engine life cycle, as verified by real flight data.

title: Recent application progress of graph neural networks in computational fluid dynamics
abstract: Traditional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) suffers from inherent numerical bottlenecks in complex geometric adaptation, unstructured mesh calculation and high-cost iterative solving, failing to balance simulation accuracy and computational efficiency for complex engineering flow problems. With the rapid development of artificial intelligence, deep learning has become a promising surrogate modelling paradigm for intelligent CFD, yet conventional grid-based methods such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are limited in representing unstructured data and multi-scale physical flow interactions. Graph neural networks (GNNs) exhibit unique structural advantages, as CFD discretization systems including meshes, particles and flux adjacency can be naturally mapped to graph topological structures and message-passing mechanisms. This review systematically summarizes the state-of-the-art GNN applications in CFD from four core optimization dimensions: graph construction, message passing, physical constraint embedding and hybrid numerical solving. The adaptive characteristics of GNNs in diverse flow scenarios, including turbulence, compressible flow, fluid-structure interaction and sparse flow field reconstruction, are further clarified. Current GNN-CFD techniques still face challenges in unified benchmark standards, complex flow generalization capability, computational overhead and physical interpretability for trustworthy engineering applications. Future research will focus on the deep integration of physics-aware graph learning and traditional numerical methods to develop scalable, stable and interpretable intelligent CFD solving systems.

title: Hybrid Physics-Informed Neural Network with Integrated Physical Constraints for Propeller Noise Prediction
abstract: With the widespread application of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in various fields, propeller noise has become a key constraint limiting their urban operations, while traditional noise prediction methods suffer from inherent flaws—empirical models prioritize efficiency over accuracy, and data-driven approaches lack physical interpretability and rely heavily on large datasets. To address these issues, this study proposes a Hybrid Physics-Informed Neural Network (HybridPINN) for propeller noise prediction. The core idea is to embed FW-H-based acoustic scaling laws in a fixed physics branch and combine them with a trainable residual corrector, thereby coupling deep learning with interpretable physical structure. To mitigate data scarcity, a data augmentation method is adopted to enhance dataset representativeness. The model features a dual-branch fusion architecture: the physics branch generates physically compliant total-noise predictions, while the data-driven branch learns residuals to compensate for systematic errors of the physical surrogate. Experimental validation shows that the framework outperforms traditional machine learning models, accurately capturing noise variation trends under the coupling of operational and geometric factors while avoiding unphysical predictions. This work provides a technical solution integrating prediction accuracy and physical interpretability, supporting the design of low-noise UAV propellers and promoting urban UAV applications.

title: Impact-induced reaction evolution in solid rocket motors: SPH simulation and physics-informed prediction
abstract: High-speed fragment impact can induce shock-driven ignition and violent reactions in solid rocket motors (SRMs), posing severe safety risks. However, the coupled effects of fragment velocity and structural size on reaction evolution remain unclear, and efficient predictive approaches are lacking. In this study, a smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) framework is developed to simulate the coupled mechanical–thermal–chemical response of SRMs under fragment impact, and is validated against light-gas gun experiments. A pressure-based criterion is proposed to distinguish shock propagation regimes and identify the onset of enhanced shock-reaction coupling. Results show that for the propellant studied in the present work a critical velocity range of 1600–1800 m s⁻¹ marks the transition from attenuating to self-amplifying shock propagation. Increasing velocity significantly enhances reaction intensity, while structural size exhibits a clear scale effect, with smaller motors promoting rapid initiation and larger motors favoring extensive reaction growth and higher reacting mass. A physics-informed Kolmogorov–Arnold network (PI-KAN) is further developed for rapid prediction of global reaction behavior, achieving high accuracy (R² = 0.96). The results provide a quantitative framework for understanding and predicting impact-induced reactions in SRMs.
